14a4728dd1b89c: You get an email from "support@securebank-alerts.com" saying your "Secure Bank" account was blocked. What's the first thing you check?
1c2e0cdad1b9d6: The bank's logo in the email — it looks professional
1a8194d82011e2: The sender's actual domain — "securebank-alerts.com" isn't the bank's official domain
07c7a20ed86935: Whether the email has spelling mistakes only
1d1bda923cb75e: A logo is easy to copy. The sender's actual domain is what can't be faked without it being noticeable — "securebank-alerts.com" is a different domain from the real bank, a classic phishing trick.
18939a45867a7e: An email asks you to "verify your account" with a button. Before clicking, you hover over the button (without clicking) and see the destination URL. What do you look for there?
0dee1940d3b11d: That the URL starts with "https://" and nothing else
15274bc0109833: That the URL's domain matches the company's real site exactly
0f31b3fdc3a0d9: No need to check anything if the button says "Verify account"
0acfd183b7385e: "https://" only means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is legitimate — even a fake site can have a padlock. What matters is that the domain matches the real one exactly.
19e3f0fd2092f5: The email subject says: "⚠️ URGENT ACTION: your account closes in 2 hours if you don't confirm your details NOW." What phishing sign is this?
1f52c4d2228e5f: None, real companies also give notices like this
14560929e76770: Urgency/fear pressure to make you act without thinking — a classic social engineering tactic
1626c28e34322a: It means the email is very important and trustworthy
0da2d3607400f6: Creating panic ("2 hours or lose your account") is a deliberate tactic: it wants you to act fast, without stopping to verify. Real companies don't usually threaten hour-long deadlines by email.
16b2dc741a356f: You get an "outstanding invoice" from a vendor you don't recognize, with a .zip file attached. What do you do?
10381d2f9aeb4d: Open it to see what it's about, out of curiosity
1ec8ab01fbb0d1: Don't open it — an unexpected attachment from an unknown sender is one of the most common ways to install malware
0498279131cc35: Forward it to a coworker to check first
0fc38dc6144fc7: Open it only if your antivirus is up to date
1ac71367c1ea14: An unexpected compressed file from someone you don't recognize is a classic red flag — many malware/ransomware attacks start exactly this way. Even the most up-to-date antivirus is no full guarantee.
1cc226ddcd4b51: An email that appears to be from your boss urgently asks you to buy gift cards and send the codes. What's the safest way to confirm it's real?
01e9f92a220317: Reply to the same email asking if it's really them
19ea56a5e3499a: Contact your boss through a DIFFERENT channel (phone, an already-known direct message) to confirm before acting
133b72867b0bd6: Buy the cards quickly so as not to keep them waiting
1df376d7d28e88: Check if the email has their name in the signature
182ed3ab088e07: Replying to the same email doesn't help — if it's phishing, you're replying to the attacker. Verifying through a completely different channel (a call, a chat you already used before) is the only reliable way to confirm identity.
0da46d211a6291: You accidentally clicked a phishing link and entered your password. What's your first step?
127500927b612b: Say nothing so you don't get in trouble
01daf1a7a68e21: Change that password right away (and anywhere else you reused it) and report it to your IT/security team
02e275a43ab8b9: Wait to see if anything bad happens before acting
18916ff453dbb9: Acting fast limits the damage: change the password (and anywhere else you reused it) and notify security so they can protect the account and warn others. Staying quiet just gives the attacker more time.
